COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on January 30, 2024, unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Trevor Moore of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as changed.[2]

The results from this Decision are Attachments A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as changed is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachments A reflect liabilities.[3]

The total sum of the tax, penalty, and interest is due and payable 20 days after a comptroller’s decision becomes final.[4] If such sum is not timely paid, an additional penalty of 10 percent of the taxes due will accrue.

SOAH Docket Nos. 304-24-01655; 304-24-01656 Suffix: 73/63

Before the State Office of Administrative Hearings

TCPA Hearing Nos. 119,606 and 119,607

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with Texas mixed beverage sales tax (MBST) and mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT) and made assessments for MBST and MBGRT sales tax, accrued interest, 10% late-filing penalty, and 50% additional penalty. Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the assessments are overstated due to errors in the average pour size for distilled spirits and average sales prices as applied in the audit and the failure to account for complimentary servings. Petitioner also contends the additional 50% penalty is not supported by the evidence, and the accrued interest should be waived. Petitioner did not provide evidence for the written submission hearing, and Staff recommended no adjustments to the assessments. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the assessments, 10% penalty, interest, and 50% additional penalty should be upheld for each assessment.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on September 21, 2023, issued Petitioner Notices of Hearing by Written Submission. On the same day, ALJ Trevor Moore issued Order Consolidating Cases and Setting Written Submission Hearing, setting the hearings and joining the cases for the purpose of issuing a single PFD. Petitioner was represented by **************. Janice Cahalane represented Staff. The contested case record closed November 30, 2023.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. Evidence

Petitioner did not submit exhibits for the hearings. Staff submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

Ninety-Day Notification Letter;

Texas Notification of Audit Results;

Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheet;

Audit Report (MBGRT);

Audit Plan (MBGRT);

Audit Report (MBST);

Audit Plan (MBST); and

Audit Report for Additional Penalty.

Staff’s exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. Staff Agreed Adjustments

Staff did not agree to adjust the assessments.

C. Material Facts

In the periods at issue, Petitioner operated a bar in CITY, Texas. In November 2021, Staff initiated an MBGRT and MBST audit of Petitioner for the period October 1, 2018, through August 31, 2021. The bar was closed at the outset of the audit.

During the audit period, Petitioner’s managers were involved in the day-to-day operations of the bar, employee INDIVIDUAL A prepared the daily deposits and the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue, and the managing member, INDIVIDUAL B, signed the returns.

At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. In response, Petitioner provided point-of-sale (POS) records. Using the available records, the auditor completed a depletion analysis audit. The depletion analysis required establishing an average pour size for each type of alcoholic beverage served at the bars, average prices, and compiling Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages.

The bar was closed at the time of the audit, and therefore a pour test could not be conducted. The auditor relied on the results from Petitioner’s prior audit, which included an unannounced pour test that resulted in an average serving size of 1.25 ounces. However, due to the various serving sizes at the bar, the auditor applied a weighted average in the audit. The 1.25 ounce serving was used for 78% of the drinks and 2.00 ounces for 22% of the drinks, resulting in a 1.515 ounce serving size (inclusive of the 0.10 spill allowance). The audits used a serving size of one serving per bottle for packaged beer and bottled wine.

Using the average pour sizes and Petitioner’s vendor‑reported purchases of alcoholic beverages reflected in the Comptroller’s Retail Inventory Tracking System (reduced to eliminate secondary liquors), the auditor calculated the number of services of each type of beverage available for sale during the audit period.

Relying on Petitioner POS reports, the auditor calculated the average selling price for each type of drink by adding the total units of each beverage type sold and the respective total receipts to calculate an average sales price for distilled spirits and beer. The average selling price of distilled spirits mixed drinks was determined to be $7.1607; the average selling price of distilled spirits bottle service was determined to be $90.6013; the average selling price of bottle wine was determined to be $328.5714; and the average selling price of packaged beer was determined to be $4.3123. Petitioner did not provide documentation of inventory losses and therefore no verified allowances were made for complimentary drinks, theft, breakage, or spills.

The number of servings available for sale were multiplied by the respective average prices to calculate the gross receipts per each beverage class. The difference between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for each beverage category was divided by the respective reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for distilled spirits and beer. The auditor applied the underreporting error percentages to reported gross receipts from drink sales and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. Those receipts were added to the reconciliation adjustments, and the applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due. Petitioner’s overall error rates were 56% for MBGRT and 54.50% for MBST.

On June 17, 2022, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for the MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments include tax, penalty for late-filed periods, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the assessments are overstated due to errors in the average pour size for distilled spirits and average sales prices as applied in the audit and the failure to account for complimentary servings. Petitioner also contends the additional 50% penalty is not supported by the evidence, and the accrued interest should be waived. Petitioner did not submit evidence for the contested case hearings.

D. ALJ’s Analysis and Recommendations

A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4). As relevant here, mixed beverage permit holders are required to prepare a service check for each individual or party served complimentary alcoholic beverages, as if it was a normal sale, but clearly marked as being complimentary. Id. §3.1001(k)(1)(E). In addition, for complimentary drinks, permit holders are required to maintain a daily summary, including complimentary alcoholic beverages dispensed, showing the number of services, type of service, kind of drink, and normal selling price. Id. §3.1001(l)(2).

In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the gross receipts tax and sales tax liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019) id.; Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

The instant audit was based upon vendor-reported purchase data, a pour test performed at Petitioner’s bar during the prior audit, and average selling prices calculated using Petitioner’s sales records as recorded in its POS system. In addition, Petitioner’s various serving sizes for distilled spirits was accounted for by applying a weighted average pour. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the audit was based on the best information available. Therefore, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e). Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the joined hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds Petitioner failed to establish error in the audit. The audit assessments should be upheld in their entirety.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, Petitioner’s overall error rates were over 50% for both mixed beverage tax types, and Petitioner provided no explanation, plausible or otherwise, for the gross underreporting. The ALJ concludes Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for each audit.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c).

In this case, Petitioner’s bar managers were involved in the day-to-day operations of the bar. Employee INDIVIDUAL A prepared the daily deposits and the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue, and the managing member, INDIVIDUAL B, signed the returns. There is no evidence that INDIVIDUAL B or Petitioner’s employees were engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of Petitioner, and Petitioner did not produce any evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner. The 50% penalty should be upheld for each assessment.

Interest is imposed on delinquent taxes beginning 60 days after the taxes are due. Tex. Tax Code §111.060(c). However, the Comptroller may waive interest upon its determination that the taxpayer exercised reasonable diligence to comply with Tax Code provisions. Tex. Tax Code §111.103 and 34 Tex. Admin. Code §3.5. When reviewing an interest waiver request, the following factors are considered: (1) undue delay caused by comptroller personnel; (2) reliance on advice provided by the comptroller’s office; and (3) natural disasters. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §3.5(e). Petitioner did not identify the applicability of any of the cited factors and therefore did not demonstrate that interest waiver is appropriate. The contention should be denied.

Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessments.

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

On September 21, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearings; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearings were to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaints or petitions filed with the state agency.

On September 21, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge issued an order setting the hearings and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single Proposal for Decision.

The contested case record closed on November 30, 2023.

Petitioner did not submit evidence for the joined hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to these hearings, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearings. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

Petitioner has not provided a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting of MBGRT and MBST.

Staff’s evidence is sufficient to demonstrate, clearly and convincingly, that the 50% penalty applied to each assessment is authorized by statute.

Signed December 1, 2023.

Trevor Moore

Presiding Administrative Law Judge
